pages.name: A known voltage
pages.text: Here is lesson 3's capacitor, 470 µF through 100 kΩ, so `RC = 47 s`, this time charged to 400 V. Its rule, `v = 400 e^(−t/47)`, is a machine. Take the time t, divide by −47, put it through eˣ, then multiply by 400. Lesson 3 ran it forwards, from a time to a voltage. Now the voltage is known and the time is not. Watch the level line come down to 75 V. By eye it crosses the curve near 80 s. Drag it to set another target.

pages.name: Which comes off first?
pages.task: The undoing machine runs the rule backwards, starting from the 75 V. Which step does it do first?
pages.why: Each step worked on what the step before handed it, so the × 400, done last, sits outside everything, and the undoing machine takes it off first. `75 ÷ 400 = 0.1875`, so `e^(−t/47) = 0.1875`, and the power stands alone. Then ln can undo eˣ, and × (−47) undoes the very first step, so it comes last. Taking ln first also works for a product, by lesson 5's product law, `ln 75 = ln 400 − t/47`, and gives the same time. It is a sum, like the cooling part's + 20 later on, that forces the order.

pages.name: Run it backwards
pages.text: The [[undoing machine]] runs along the bottom, last step first. `75 ÷ 400 = 0.1875`, so the power stands alone. ln undoes eˣ, giving −1.674, and × (−47) undoes the ÷ (−47), giving 78.7 s. That lands exactly under the crossing, and the level line agrees by eye. A trade page reports that the IEC 60831 standard requires discharge to below 75 V within 3 minutes, and 78.7 s is inside that. But the standard is for power capacitor banks, and a worked-out time proves nothing: prove it dead with a tester before you touch it. Drag the level line and the machine follows.

pages.name: Down to 200 V
pages.task: How long does the capacitor take to fall to 200 V?
pages.why: `200 ÷ 400 = 0.5`, so `e^(−t/47) = 0.5`. ln gives `ln 0.5 ≈ −0.693`, and × (−47) gives about 32.6 s. That is `47 × ln 2`, with `ln 2 ≈ 0.693`. The curve falls fastest at the start and then slows, so keeping up the starting pace would get there too soon, at 23.5 s.

pages.name: Both sides
pages.text: In symbols, each step is done to both sides, as in Solving equations. Dividing both sides by 400 leaves the power standing alone. Then take ln of both sides. By the power law `ln(e^k) = k × ln e`, and `ln e = 1`, so ln takes the e away and leaves its power. Multiplying both sides by −47 gives the time. Drag the level line and the lines follow.

pages.task: From `0.1875 = e^(−t/47)`, which line comes next?
pages.why: ln undoes eˣ, so take ln of both sides. By the power law `ln(e^(−t/47)) = (−t/47) × ln e`, and `ln e = 1`, which leaves `ln 0.1875 = −t/47`. log is base 10, and `log e ≈ 0.434`, not 1, so log would leave `0.434 × (−t/47)` on the right.

pages.name: Any base
pages.text: An equation with the unknown in a power is an [[exponential equation]], and the same steps work in any base. In `2^x = 20` the power already stands alone, so take log of both sides. By the power law `log(2^x) = x log 2`, so `x log 2 = log 20`, and the unknown has come down. Divide by log 2, and `x = 1.301 ÷ 0.301 ≈ 4.32`. Check it, `2^4.32 ≈ 20`, just where the level line crosses the curve. Any log works if you keep the log of the base, so ln would do as well, `ln 20 ÷ ln 2 ≈ 4.32`. ln is the tidy one for e because `ln e = 1`.

pages.name: Doubling at 5%
pages.task: Money grows by 5% a year, so after x years it is `1.05^x` times the start. How long does it take to double?
pages.why: Take log of both sides of `1.05^x = 2`. By the power law `x log 1.05 = log 2`, so `x = 0.301 ÷ 0.0212 ≈ 14.2` years. Each year's 5% is 5% of a bigger amount, so it doubles sooner than the 20 years that adding 5% of the first amount would take. The rule of 72 checks it, `72 ÷ 5 = 14.4` years, close to the exact 14.2.

pages.name: Cooling, last step first
pages.text: Lesson 3's part, at 90 °C in a 20 °C room with τ = 10 minutes, follows `T = 20 + 70 e^(−t/10)`. When is it at 30 °C? Its machine's last step is + 20, so the undoing machine takes 20 away first, `30 − 20 = 10`. Then ÷ 70 gives 0.143, ln gives −1.946, and × (−10) gives about 19.5 minutes, just before lesson 3's 29.5 °C at 20 minutes.

pages.name: The first step here
pages.task: The part is to reach 30 °C. What is the first step?
pages.why: The forward machine ends with + 20, so the 20 sits outside everything and comes off first, `30 − 20 = 10`. Take ln straight away and you meet `ln(20 + 70 e^(−t/10))`, the log of a sum, which no log law splits, so the power stays stuck inside. Next comes ÷ 70, then ln, then × (−10).

pages.name: An unknown inside a log
pages.text: When the unknown sits inside a log, it is a [[logarithmic equation]]. Turn the log form into the power form, as in lesson 4. `log x = 1.5` means x sits 1.5 spaces along the power ruler, at `10^1.5 ≈ 31.6`. Two logs added are first joined by the product law, so `log x + log(x + 3) = 1` becomes `x(x + 3) = 10`. Take 10 from both sides, `x² + 3x − 10 = 0`, and `(x + 5)(x − 2) = 0` gives 2 or −5. Left of 1 the ruler's numbers shrink towards 0 and never reach it, so it has no place for −5: no power of 10 is negative. So only 2 is a solution. Check it, `log 2 + log 5 = 1`.

pages.name: Two logs
pages.why: By the product law `log(x(x − 3)) = 1`, so `x(x − 3) = 10`, that is `x² − 3x − 10 = 0`, or `(x − 5)(x + 2) = 0`. That gives 5 or −2. −2 would need `log(−2)`, which does not exist, so `x = 5` only. Check it, `log 5 + log 2 = 1`.

pages.name: Halving every 10 s
pages.task: Lesson 1's capacitor starts at 400 V and halves every 10 s, so `v = 400 × 0.5^(t/10)`. When is it down to 30 V?
pages.why: Divide by 400, `0.5^(t/10) = 0.075`. Take log of both sides, and by the power law `(t ÷ 10) × log 0.5 = log 0.075`, so `t ÷ 10 = (−1.125) ÷ (−0.301) ≈ 3.74` halvings, two negatives making a positive, and `t ≈ 37.4 s`, between the 30 and 40 seconds lesson 1 found.

pages.name: Checking once a minute
pages.task: Back to lesson 3's capacitor, with the level line at 30 V. Checked once a minute, at which check is it first below 30 V?
pages.why: `30 ÷ 400 = 0.075`, `ln 0.075 ≈ −2.590`, and × (−47) gives 121.7 s, just after 2 minutes. At the 2-minute check it still reads 31.1 V, so the first check below 30 V is at 3 minutes. Rounding a waiting time down is the slip to watch for.
